summary: This work introduces a static neutral-atom architecture using auxiliary mediator atoms to enable long-range entangling gates via Rydberg interactions, eliminating transport-induced heating and latency that scales with code distance. Through co-designed optimal-control pulses achieving $F \approx 0.999$ fidelity over hundreds of nanoseconds and large-scale error-correction simulations, the architecture demonstrates more than order-of-magnitude improvements in logical error rates compared to atom-shuttling approaches for surface codes ($d \lesssim 12$) and high-rate LDPC codes.
motivation: Neutral-atom quantum computers require scalable long-range connectivity for efficient quantum error correction, but atom transport introduces motional heating with infidelity scaling as $\mathcal{O}(d^{2/3})$ and latency scaling as $\mathcal{O}(d^{1/3})$ that severely limits logical performance in large systems.
method: Bus-mediated controlled-$Z$ gates between distant qubits are optimized using Gradient Ascent Pulse Engineering (GRAPE), incorporating microscopic Rydberg dynamics and architectural constraints. Pulses are co-designed with interaction-flatness constraints to suppress motional errors, then benchmarked against atom-shuttling architectures via numerical simulations of surface codes, La-cross codes, and bivariate bicycle codes under realistic noise models including spontaneous emission, thermal motion, and motion-induced dephasing.
result: Time-optimal bus-mediated gates achieve fidelities approaching 99.9% with durations of a few hundred nanoseconds for code distances up to $d=11$ ($r_0 \approx 2.6$ µm, $n_{\rm Rb/Cs} \approx 73-78$, $\Omega_{\max}=2\pi \times 2$ MHz); logical gate times are $\sim 100$ µs and QEC cycles $\sim 1$ ms for $d \lesssim 12$, achieving over an order-of-magnitude reduction in logical error rates at $p \sim 10^{-3}$ compared to shuttling-based implementations.
